summary: This Wikipedia-derived note describes the compact city (or city of short distances), an urban planning concept promoting relatively high residential density, mixed land uses, efficient public transport, and walkable layouts to reduce car dependence and environmental impact. It covers the concept's origins, key terms, links to smart growth and sustainability, debates over whether compact cities truly deliver sustainability benefits, the paradox of intensification, and case studies from Australia and Belgium, plus proposed improvements and European policy influence.
one_line: Overview of the compact city concept in urban planning: high-density, mixed-use, transit-oriented development aimed at reducing car dependence and environmental impact, and its debated sustainability outcomes.
key_facts: The compact city or city of short distances is an urban planning and urban design concept that promotes relatively high residential density with mixed land uses.
The compact city is based on an efficient public transport system and is said by its advocates to encourage walking and cycling, low energy consumption and reduced pollution.
The term compact city was first coined in 1973 by mathematicians George Dantzig and Thomas L. Saaty.
The concept is often attributed to Jane Jacobs and her 1961 book The Death and Life of Great American Cities.
Jacobs argued four conditions were necessary for urban diversity: mixed uses, small walkable blocks, mingling of building ages and types, and a sufficiently dense concentration of people.
The note states that a hundred dwellings per acre (247 per hectare) could be considered a minimum density for diversity, high by American standards but common in European and Asian cities.
Self-sustaining means a city has everything a person needs within the community, including stores, employers, a post office, service providers, energy generation and waste processing.
A study by Boussauw et al. found that shorter commutes correlate with high values for density, diversity, and job accessibility.

Rérat identified three criticisms of the compact city model: supply and demand alignment is not always feasible, higher living costs push lower-income families to the outskirts, and environmental impacts from dense waste and pollution are significant.
An influential 1989 study by Peter Newman and Jeff Kenworthy compared 32 cities across North America, Australia, Europe and Asia.

Melia et al. (2011) proposed the paradox of intensification: urban intensification increases population density and reduces per capita car use but also increases concentrations of motor traffic locally.
The note states that doubling the population density of an area will not halve the frequency or distance of car use.

Portland, Oregon substantially increased its population density between 1990 and 2000 while other similar-sized US cities were reducing in density, and traffic and congestion rose more rapidly than in those cities.
Freiburg im Breisgau in Germany is cited as a city more successful at counteracting traffic increases from higher density.
Australia adopted the compact city model for all its urban planning beginning in 2000, with objectives including limiting urban sprawl and encouraging walking and cycling.
The European Commission published the Green Paper Towards a new culture for urban mobility on 27 September 2007.
The European Parliament's Resolution of 9 July 2008 called for sustainable mobility plans for a 'city of short distances'.
